It is found in Europe, western Siberia, Asia Minor, the Caucusus and North Africa.{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=10IMFSavIMsC&pg=PA417 |page=417 |title=Mansfeld's Encyclopedia of Agricultural and Horticultural Crops: (Except Ornamentals) |author=Peter Hanelt |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |year=2001|isbn=978-3-540-41017-1 }} It prefers dry [[pasture]]s, mostly on lime rich soils.{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xWqLEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA316 |page=316 |title=Plant Atlas 2020: Mapping Changes in the Distribution of the British and Irish Flora |author1=P. Accessed July 2013 ==Taxonomy and naming== The [[genus name]] ''Filipendula'' comes from Latin {{Lang|la|filum}} ("thread") and {{Lang|la|pendulus}} ("hanging") in reference to the [[root tuber]]s that hang from the roots in some species. The [[specific epithet]] ''vulgaris'' means "common". The English name "dropwort" comes from the tubers that hang like drops from the root. The species was first described in the literature in 1794 by [[Conrad Moench]] in ''Methodus Plantas''.{{cite book |last=Moench |first=Conrado |date=1794 |title=Methodus Plantas: Horti Botanici et Agri Marburgensis, a Staminum Situ Describendi |trans-title=Methods in Plants: Botanical Gardens and Fields of Marburg, a Description of the Situation of the Stamens |language=Latin |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/449294 |location=Marburg |publisher= Marburgi Cattorum: Nova Libraria Academiae|page=663 |access-date=2025-04-12}} ==Description== It has finely-cut, fern-like radical leaves which form a basal rosette, and an erect stem {{Convert|20|-|50|cm|in|sigfig=1}} tall[[C. A. Stace]], ''Interactive Flora of the British Isles, a Digital Encyclopaedia'': ''Filipendula vulgaris''. {{ISBN|90-75000-69-3}}. ([http://nlbif.eti.uva.nl/bis/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=2599 Online version)] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110608014356/http://nlbif.eti.uva.nl/bis/flora.php?selected=beschrijving&menuentry=soorten&id=2599 |date=2011-06-08 }} bearing a loose terminal [[inflorescence]] of small creamy white flowers. The flowers appear in dense clusters from late spring to midsummer atop sparsely leafed stems. The plant has an overall height of {{Convert|50|-|100|cm|in|sigfig=1}}, achieved after 2–5 years, and a spread of around about {{Convert|10|-|50|cm|in|sigfig=1}}.{{Cite web |title=Filipendula vulgaris {{!}} dropwort Herbaceous Perennial/RHS |author= |work=[[Royal Horticultural Society]] |date= |access-date=26 January 2025 |url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/7226/filipendula-vulgaris/details |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250126021046/https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/7226/filipendula-vulgaris/details |archive-date=26 January 2025}} This plant prefers full sun or partial shade. It is more tolerant of dry conditions than most other members of its genus. It is a perennial of chalk and limestone downs and on heaths on other basic rocks. ==Cultivation== [[Plant propagation|Propagation]] is by seed and the division of the creeping roots. The tuberous roots and young leaves can be cooked as a vegetable or eaten raw as a salad. The taste is bitter sweet. The mature leaves smell of oil of [[wintergreen]] when crushed, due to the release of [[methyl salicylate]].
